claim: BiP is the only Hsp70 chaperone in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: BiP is the only Hsp70 chaperone in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and similar to other Hsp70s, its activity relies on nucleotide- and substrate-controllable docking and undocking of its nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) and substrate-binding domain (SBD).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and introduction, supported by citations to literature (Araki and Nagata, 2011; Vincenz-Donnelly and Hipp, 2017).

claim: BiP activity relies on nucleotide- and substrate-controllable docking and undocking of its nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) and substrate-binding domain (SBD).
source: BiP is the only Hsp70 chaperone in the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and similar to other Hsp70s, its activity relies on nucleotide- and substrate-controllable docking and undocking of its nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) and substrate-binding domain (SBD).
evidence: This is a general statement about BiP mechanism, supported by comparison to other Hsp70s and established knowledge in the field.

claim: ATP-bound BiP exhibits surprising conformational heterogeneity that distinguishes BiP from its bacterial homologue DnaK.
source: We present methyl NMR analysis of the BiP chaperone cycle that reveals surprising conformational heterogeneity of ATP-bound BiP that distinguishes BiP from its bacterial homologue DnaK.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the methyl NMR experiments presented in the manuscript, particularly shown in Figure 2.

claim: BiP inactivation by AMPylation of its SBD does not disturb Hsp70 inter-domain allostery and preserves BiP structure.
source: In particular, BiP inactivation by AMPylation of its SBD does not disturb Hsp70 inter-domain allostery and preserves BiP structure.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data showing that AMPylation affects conformational equilibrium without disrupting the structure, as shown in Figure 5 and related supplementary figures.

claim: AMPylation of BiP relies on a redistribution of the BiP conformational ensemble and stabilization of the domain-docked conformation in presence of ADP and ATP.
source: Instead it relies on a redistribution of the BiP conformational ensemble and stabilization the domain-docked conformation in presence of ADP and ATP.
evidence: This is demonstrated by NMR peak intensity analysis showing increased population of domain-docked conformation upon AMPylation, as shown in Figure 5A.

claim: BiP binds to the majority of unfolded and misfolded proteins in the ER to promote their folding and prevent aggregation.
source: BiP binds to the majority of unfolded and misfolded proteins in this organelle to promote their folding and prevent aggregation (Araki and Nagata, 2011; Vincenz-Donnelly and Hipp, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature establishing BiP's role in protein quality control.

claim: BiP shares about 60% of its sequence identity with E. coli Hsp70 (DnaK) and human cytosolic Hsp70s.
source: BiP belongs to the highly conserved Hsp70 chaperone family and shares about 60% of its sequence identity with E. coli Hsp70 (DnaK) and human cytosolic Hsp70s (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a factual statement about sequence homology supported by citation.

claim: BiP and other Hsp70s have identical domain organization consisting of a C-terminal substrate-binding domain (SBD) and an N-terminal nucleotide-binding domain (NBD), which are attached by a highly conserved hydrophobic linker.
source: BiP and other Hsp70s have identical domain organization (Behnke et al., 2015) (Figure 1): They consist of a C-terminal substrate-binding domain (SBD) and an N-terminal nucleotide-binding domain (NDB), which are attached by a highly conserved hydrophobic linker.
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1 showing the domain structure.

claim: The SBD is made of a β-sandwich domain (βSBD) and a α-helical lid (αLid).
source: The SBD, which in turn, is made of a β-sandwich domain (βSBD) and a α-helical lid (αLid), binds to unfolded protein substrates, while the NBD is an ATPase that regulates the affinity of substrate binding to the SBD by using energy from ATP hydrolysis (Mayer et al., 2001; Mayer, 2013).
evidence: This is a structural description supported by citations and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The NBD is an ATPase that regulates the affinity of substrate binding to the SBD by using energy from ATP hydrolysis.
source: The SBD, which in turn, is made of a β-sandwich domain (βSBD) and a α-helical lid (αLid), binds to unfolded protein substrates, while the NBD is an ATPase that regulates the affinity of substrate binding to the SBD by using energy from ATP hydrolysis (Mayer et al., 2001; Mayer, 2013).
evidence: This is a mechanistic description of NBD function supported by citations.

claim: In DnaK, ATP binding favors a compact, domain-docked, linker-bound conformation, which has low ATPase activity.
source: In DnaK, ATP binding favors a compact, domain-docked, linker-bound conformation, which has low ATPase activity (Zhuravleva et al., 2012; Kityk et al., 2012; Qi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about DnaK mechanism supported by multiple citations.

claim: Substrate binding to ATP-bound DnaK stabilizes a transient domain-undocked, linker-bound state, which has enhanced ATPase activity, efficient substrate binding and release kinetics, and low substrate affinity.
source: Substrate binding to this state stabilizes a transient domain-undocked, linker-bound state, which has enhanced ATPase activity, efficient (fast) substrate binding and release kinetics, and low substrate affinity (Zhuravleva et al., 2012; Lai et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes DnaK conformational transitions upon substrate binding, supported by citations.

claim: ATP hydrolysis in DnaK results in stabilization of the domain-undocked, linker-unbound state, which has high substrate affinity, but very slow and inefficient substrate binding and release.
source: ATP hydrolysis (converting ATP to ADP), results in stabilization of the domain-undocked, linker-unbound state, which has high substrate affinity, but very slow and inefficient substrate binding and release (Bertelsen et al., 2009a; Swain et al., 2007).
evidence: This describes the ADP-bound state of DnaK, supported by citations.

claim: In the domain-undocked (ADP-bound) conformation, the two Hsp70 domains behave independently and are structurally identical to the isolated NBD and SBD.
source: In the domain-undocked (ADP-bound) conformation, the two Hsp70 domains behave independently and are structurally identical to the isolated NBD and SBD (Zhuravleva et al., 2012; Bertelsen et al., 2009a; Swain et al., 2007) (Figure 1, left).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: X-ray and NMR structures of the isolated Hsp70 domains (including those for BiP) are almost identical, independent of ligand-bound status and organism.
source: Remarkably, for a number of different Hsp70s, X-ray and NMR structures of the isolated domains (including those for BiP) are almost identical, independent of ligand-bound status and organism (Mayer and Kityk, 2015; Wisniewska et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparative structural observation supported by multiple citations.

claim: Recent X-ray structures of ATP-bound DnaK and human BiP revealed only subtle differences in the domain-docked conformation for these two chaperones.
source: Moreover, recent X-ray structures of ATP-bound DnaK (Kityk et al., 2012; Qi et al., 2013) and human BiP (Yang et al., 2015) revealed only subtle differences in the domain-docked conformation for these two chaperones
evidence: This is a comparative structural statement supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: In both ATP-bound DnaK and BiP structures, the interdomain linker binds to the NBD.
source: In both structures the interdomain linker binds to the NBD; the βSBD and NBD are docked to each other with the αLid detached from the βSBD and interacting with the NBD; whilst the βSBD is opened, making the βSBD pocket solvent accessible and ready to bind to a client protein (Yang et al., 2015) (Figure 1, right).
evidence: This is a structural description supported by citation and shown in Figure 1.

claim: In ATP-bound DnaK and BiP, the βSBD and NBD are docked to each other with the αLid detached from the βSBD and interacting with the NBD.
source: In both structures the interdomain linker binds to the NBD; the βSBD and NBD are docked to each other with the αLid detached from the βSBD and interacting with the NBD; whilst the βSBD is opened, making the βSBD pocket solvent accessible and ready to bind to a client protein (Yang et al., 2015) (Figure 1, right).
evidence: This is a structural description supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: In ATP-bound DnaK and BiP, the βSBD is opened, making the βSBD pocket solvent accessible and ready to bind to a client protein.
source: In both structures the interdomain linker binds to the NBD; the βSBD and NBD are docked to each other with the αLid detached from the βSBD and interacting with the NBD; whilst the βSBD is opened, making the βSBD pocket solvent accessible and ready to bind to a client protein (Yang et al., 2015) (Figure 1, right).
evidence: This is a structural and functional description supported by citation.

claim: The functional activity of different Hsp70s, including DnaK and BiP, varies very significantly.
source: Despite this structural similarity, the functional activity of different Hsp70s, including DnaK and BiP, varies very significantly (Behnke et al., 2015; Bonomo et al., 2010) in response to differences in the protein-folding environment for different Hsp70s and the wide range of variations in substrates and their specificity.
evidence: This is supported by citations comparing functional activities of different Hsp70s.

claim: Hsp70 chaperones are extremely flexible in solution and crystallographic data have provided only 'end-point' snapshots of the chaperone landscape.
source: Growing evidence has suggested that Hsp70 chaperones are extremely flexible in solution and crystallographic data have provided only 'end-point' snapshots of the chaperone landscape (Zhuravleva et al., 2012; Lai et al., 2017; Zhuravleva and Gierasch, 2015; Zhuravleva and Gierasch, 2011; Marcinowski et al., 2011a; Bhattacharya et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a general statement about Hsp70 dynamics supported by multiple citations.

claim: Transitions between Hsp70 conformational states and chaperone conformational dynamics have been hypothesized to be key factors that control the Hsp70 functional cycle.
source: In turn, transitions between these 'end-point' states and chaperone conformational dynamics have been recently hypothesized to be key factors that control the Hsp70 functional cycle (Zhuravleva et al., 2012; Kityk et al., 2012; Zhuravleva and Gierasch, 2015; Kityk et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to recent work.

claim: A thermodynamic distribution between different DnaK conformations is under precise adjustments by regulatory regions (allosteric 'hotspots').
source: Indeed, a thermodynamic distribution between different DnaK conformations, and thus its ATPase activity and substrate binding and release, are under precise adjustments by regulatory regions (allosteric 'hotspots') that enable regulation of DnaK conformational transitions.
evidence: This is supported by previous work on DnaK allostery.

claim: Subtle perturbations at DnaK allosteric hotspots affect and fine-tune the DnaK conformational cycle and adjust its chaperone activity.
source: Even subtle perturbations (such as amino-acid substitutions or ligand binding) at these allosteric hotspots have been shown to affect and fine-tune the DnaK conformational cycle and adjust its chaperone activity (Zhuravleva et al., 2012; Zhuravleva and Gierasch, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Many allosteric hotspots are not fully conserved among Hsp70 family members.
source: Remarkably, many allosteric hotspots are not fully conserved (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), suggesting a plausible molecular mechanism for functional diversity within the Hsp70 family as well as for real-time regulations of Hsp70 activity post-translationally, for example, through covalent modifications and/or interactions with co-chaperones (Zhuravleva et al., 2012; Kityk et al., 2012; Zhuravleva and Gierasch, 2015; Kityk et al., 2015; Ahmad et al., 2011; Mapa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: The T229G mutation in BiP slows down protein ATPase activity.
source: All of the experiments were performed using a well-established variant of wild-type (WT) BiP (referred as BiP* in this paper), in which Thr 229 was mutated to Gly to slow down protein ATPase activity (Wei et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous characterization of this mutant.

claim: The T229G variant of BiP retains WT-like conformational features.
source: The T229G variant of BiP has been extensively characterized in the literature and retains WT-like conformational features (Wei et al., 1995; Wei and Hendershot, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous characterization.

claim: Nucleotide binding to BiP occurred with weaker µM affinity than for DnaK.
source: Our ITC data (Table 1) showed that nucleotide binding to BiP occurred with weaker µM affinity than for DnaK and in general agreed with previous observations (Wei and Hendershot, 1995; Macias et al., 2011; Lamb et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Table 1 and citations to previous work.

claim: ATP binding to BiP* was near 7-fold more preferable than ADP binding.
source: In our hands, ATP binding to BiP* was near 7-fold more preferable than ADP binding (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on ITC measurements shown in Table 1.

claim: Upon truncation of the interdomain linker and SBD, ATP affinity of the isolated NBD* decreased more than nine times as compared with FL BiP*.
source: Interestingly, upon truncation of the interdomain linker and SBD, ATP affinity of the isolated NBD* decreased more than nine times as compared with FL BiP*.
evidence: This is based on ITC data comparing full-length and truncated constructs shown in Table 1.

claim: The truncation of the SBD only (without the linker truncation) results in a diminished effect on ATP affinity.
source: However, the truncation of the SBD only (i.e., without the linker truncation) results in a diminished effect (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on ITC data comparing different truncation constructs shown in Table 1.

claim: Domain communication and/or linker-NBD interactions play an important stabilizing role for ATP binding to BiP.
source: Taken together, these observations suggested an important stabilizing role of domain communication and/or linker-NBD interactions for ATP binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the ITC data comparing different constructs.

claim: ATP (but not ADP) binding to FL BiP* was entropically driven with the contribution from the entropy (-T∆S) to the binding energy of about −19–20 kcal/mol.
source: ATP (but not ADP) binding to FL BiP* was entropically driven with the contribution from the entropy (-T∆S) to the binding energy of about −19–20 kcal/mol (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on thermodynamic analysis of ITC data shown in Table 1.

claim: ATP binding to the isolated BiP NBD* is predominantly entropically driven.
source: On the contrary, ATP binding to the isolated BiP NBD* is predominantly entropically driven (Table 1), suggesting that ATP binding to BiP and DnaK has different effects on chaperone dynamics.
evidence: This is based on ITC data shown in Table 1.

claim: ATP binding to BiP resulted in enhanced linker-induced intradomain flexibility in its NBD, while ATP binding to DnaK affected the entire protein.
source: In contrast to DnaK, ATP binding to BiP resulted in enhanced linker-induced intradomain flexibility in its NBD, while ATP binding to DnaK affected the entire protein.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of thermodynamic data between BiP and DnaK.

claim: In the absence of ATP (i.e., in the ADP-bound state), almost no changes in methyl NMR peak positions were observed between FL BiP* and its isolated NBD and SBD.
source: Consistent with DnaK, (Zhuravleva et al., 2012; Swain et al., 2007; Bertelsen et al., 2009b) in the absence of ATP (i.e., in the ADP-bound state), we observed almost no changes in methyl NMR peak positions between FL BiP* and its isolated NBD and SBD (Figure 2, left).
evidence: This is based on NMR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: ADP-bound BiP lacks domain communication, the two BiP domains behave independently, and the protein adopts the domain-undocked conformation.
source: This suggests that ADP-bound BiP lacks domain communication, the two BiP domains behave independently, and the protein adopts the domain-undocked conformation (Figure 1, left).
evidence: This is inferred from NMR data showing no chemical shift differences between full-length and isolated domains.

claim: ATP binding to FL BiP* drastically affected the methyl peak pattern and the resulting NMR spectrum possessed two sets of peaks with near identical peak intensities.
source: ATP binding to FL BiP* drastically affected the methyl peak pattern and the resulting NMR spectrum possessed two sets of peaks with near identical peak intensities (Figure 2, right), suggesting that two BiP conformations, interconverting on the slow NMR time-scale, co-existed in solution.
evidence: This is based on NMR data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Two BiP conformations, interconverting on the slow NMR time-scale, co-existed in solution in the presence of ATP.
source: ATP binding to FL BiP* drastically affected the methyl peak pattern and the resulting NMR spectrum possessed two sets of peaks with near identical peak intensities (Figure 2, right), suggesting that two BiP conformations, interconverting on the slow NMR time-scale, co-existed in solution.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of two sets of peaks in NMR spectra.

claim: In the presence of ATP, only ~53 ± 7% of BiP molecules adopt the domain-docked conformation, while the rest of the protein is domain-undocked.
source: This analysis revealed that in the presence of ATP, only ~53 ± 7% of BiP molecules adopt the domain-docked conformation, while the rest of the protein is domain-undocked.
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of NMR peak intensities.

claim: Interconversion between the domain-undocked and -docked conformation in BiP is significantly slower than ~50 milliseconds.
source: Taking into account that chemical shift differences between the domain-undocked and -docked conformations were less than 0.03 ppm (0.4 ppm) for 1H (13C) chemical shifts and no significant line broadening was observed in the methyl NMR spectrum, we estimated that interconversion between the domain-undocked and -docked conformation is significantly slower that ~50 milliseconds (estimated as the slow exchange limit with the respect to the chemical shift differences between the two conformations).
evidence: This is estimated from NMR spectral properties (chemical shift differences and line widths).

claim: Domain docking in BiP is a multistep process that requires very large structural rearrangements.
source: Such slow motions (and thus a large activation energy of the domain docking process) is not unexpected, given that domain docking is a multistep process that requires very large structural rearrangements (e.g., the αLid displacements are on a scale of ~10 nanometers, Figure 1) (Kityk et al., 2012; Qi et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from structural data and supported by citations.

claim: Domain docking in DnaK is a significantly faster process than in BiP as reported by a characteristic linear peak-walking pattern in DnaK NMR spectra.
source: Interestingly, domain docking in DnaK is a significantly faster process as reported by a characteristic linear peak-walking pattern in DnaK NMR spectra, observed upon the gradual population of the domain-docked conformation (Zhuravleva et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on comparison to previous NMR studies of DnaK.

claim: Binding of the model peptide substrate (P2: HTFPAVL) to ATP-bound BiP* destabilized domain docking.
source: Similar to DnaK, (Zhuravleva et al., 2012) binding of the model peptide substrate (P2: HTFPAVL [Marcinowski et al., 2011b]) to ATP-bound BiP* destabilized domain docking (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: ATP binding to the isolated BiP NBD favors linker interactions with the NBD.
source: Taken together, these observations clearly demonstrate that similar to DnaK, ATP binding to the isolated BiP NBD favors linker interactions with the NBD and the presence of the linker and ATP results in allosteric changes in the NBD.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR data comparing constructs with and without the linker.

claim: The presence of the linker and ATP results in allosteric changes in the BiP NBD.
source: Taken together, these observations clearly demonstrate that similar to DnaK, ATP binding to the isolated BiP NBD favors linker interactions with the NBD and the presence of the linker and ATP results in allosteric changes in the NBD.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR chemical shift perturbations observed when comparing constructs with and without the linker.

claim: For BiP, no significant amount of the linker-bound, domain-undocked conformation was observed for the FL BiP*.
source: However, for BiP no significant amount of the linker-bound, domain-undocked conformation was observed for the FL BiP*.
evidence: This is based on NMR spectral analysis showing that domain-undocked peaks in FL BiP overlap with isolated NBD without linker.

claim: The enhanced conformational heterogeneity of BiP enables post-translational regulation of BiP activity and function.
source: We hypothesize that the enhanced conformational heterogeneity of BiP enables post-translational regulation of BiP activity and function.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the experimental findings about BiP conformational ensemble.

claim: Local perturbations of the BiP SBD via 'soft' single-site amino acid substitutions enable allosteric controlling of the BiP conformational ensemble.
source: Our findings illustrate that local perturbations of the BiP SBD via 'soft' single-site amino acid substitutions enable allosteric controlling of the BiP conformational ensemble (Figure 6, right).
evidence: This is based on NMR data showing that mutations affect the population of domain-docked and -undocked conformations, as shown in Figure 4.

claim: The V461F and I526V substitutions favor the domain-docked conformation in BiP.
source: Indeed, the V461F (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2) and I526V (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) substitutions favors domain docking, while the I437V (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) and I538V (Figure 4—figure supplement 5) substitutions stabilizes the domain-undocked conformation.
evidence: This is based on NMR data showing increased population of domain-docked conformation for these mutants, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The I437V and I538V substitutions stabilize the domain-undocked conformation in BiP.
source: Indeed, the V461F (Figure 4—figure supplements 1 and 2) and I526V (Figure 4—figure supplement 4) substitutions favors domain docking, while the I437V (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) and I538V (Figure 4—figure supplement 5) substitutions stabilizes the domain-undocked conformation.
evidence: This is based on NMR data showing decreased population of domain-docked conformation for these mutants, as shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Even in the absence of ATP, the domain-docked conformation is significantly populated for BiP*-V461F (~49%) and BiP*-I526V (~35%).
source: Moreover, even in the absence of ATP, the domain-docked conformation is significantly populated for BiP*-V461F (~49%) and BiP*-I526V (~35%) (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting that ATP binding is not an essential step for domain docking.
evidence: This is based on NMR data showing domain-docked conformation in ADP-bound state for these mutants.

claim: ATP binding is not an essential step for domain docking in BiP.
source: Moreover, even in the absence of ATP, the domain-docked conformation is significantly populated for BiP*-V461F (~49%) and BiP*-I526V (~35%) (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4, and Figure 4—source data 1), suggesting that ATP binding is not an essential step for domain docking.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR data showing domain docking can occur in ADP-bound state.

claim: The AMPylation site Thr518 is located on the loop L7,8 of the βSBD that connects allosterically important strands β7 and β8.
source: The AMPylation site Thr518 is located on the loop L7,8 of the βSBD that connects allosterically important strands β7 and β8 (Figure 4A), an allosteric region that controls βSBD conformation in DnaK (Zhuravleva and Gierasch, 2015).
evidence: This is a structural description shown in Figure 4A and supported by citation.

claim: AMPylation of Thr518 shifts the BiP conformational equilibrium toward the domain-docked conformation in the presence of ATP (68% of the docked conformation).
source: Our results suggested that AMPylation of the loop L7,8 has a similar effect as the I526V substitution in the strand β8 and the V461F substitution in the substrate-binding site: It shifts the BiP conformational equilibrium toward the domain-docked conformation in the presence of ATP (68% of the docked conformation), but also significantly stabilizes the domain docking in the absence of ATP (64% of the docked conformation, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on NMR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: AMPylation of Thr518 significantly stabilizes domain docking in the absence of ATP (64% of the docked conformation).
source: Our results suggested that AMPylation of the loop L7,8 has a similar effect as the I526V substitution in the strand β8 and the V461F substitution in the substrate-binding site: It shifts the BiP conformational equilibrium toward the domain-docked conformation in the presence of ATP (68% of the docked conformation), but also significantly stabilizes the domain docking in the absence of ATP (64% of the docked conformation, Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is based on NMR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: AMPylation of WT BiP* was incomplete (~60%).
source: Indeed, in our hands, AMPylation of WT BiP* was incomplete (~60%, Figure 5—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7.

claim: The V461F substitution made AMPylation near 100% efficient.
source: To achieve sample homogeneity, we also performed the experiments on the V461F BiP* variant, which made AMPyaltion near 100% efficient (Figure 5—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 7.

claim: AMPylated BiP*-V461F predominantly (>80%) adopts the domain-docked conformation in the presence of either ATP or ADP.
source: As a result, AMPylated BiP*-V461F predominantly (>80%) adopts the domain-docked conformation in the presence of either ATP or ADP (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on NMR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No chemical shift differences were observed in methyl NMR spectra for the peaks corresponding to the BiP domain-docked conformation, regardless of whether BiP* or its V461F variant were ATP-bound and non-AMPylated, ATP-bound and AMPylated or ADP-bound and AMPylated.
source: Remarkably, no chemical shift differences were observed in methyl NMR spectra for the peaks corresponding to the BiP domain-docked conformation, regardless either the BiP* or its V461F variant were ATP-bound and non-AMPylated, ATP-bound and AMPylated or ADP-bound and AMPylated.
evidence: This is based on comparison of NMR spectra shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: When the domain-docked conformation became predominantly populated for the AMPylated V461F variant, the methyl spectra of ADP-bound and ATP-bound conformation were almost identical.
source: Moreover, then the domain-docked conformation became predominantly populated for the AMPylated V461F variant, the methyl spectra of ADP-bound and ATP-bound conformation were almost identical (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), while only a few minor (local) chemical shift perturbations were observed in amide NMR spectra (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on NMR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: AMPylation stabilizes the structurally same domain-docked BiP conformation that is normally observed upon ATP binding.
source: These results are in excellent agreement with the biochemical and structural study of AMPylated BiP, where linker-specific proteolysis and X-ray crystallography was used to demonstrate that, in the absence of ATP, AMPylation stabilizes the structurally same domain-docked BiP conformation that is normally observed upon ATP binding (Preissler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a structural study and consistent with the NMR data.

claim: Stabilization of the domain-docked conformation gradually increases the ADP and ATP binding energy.
source: Our results demonstrate that stabilization of the domain-docked conformation gradually increases the ADP and ATP binding energy (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on analysis of ITC and NMR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The correlation between the free energies of domain docking and nucleotide binding can be quantitatively rationalized by considering BiP as an ensemble of two thermodynamically distinct states.
source: This correlation between the free energies of domain docking and nucleotide binding can be quantitatively rationalized by considering kinetics and thermodynamics of the multistep ATP-induced conformational transitions in the BiP molecule. The simplest model, in which the BiP co-exists as an ensemble of two thermodynamically distinct states, was suitable to fit the experimental data (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on thermodynamic modeling of the experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The best agreement with the experimental data was achieved when ATP (ADP) binding constants were 800 nM (7 μM) and 1 nM (1.5 μM) for the domain-undocked and –docked states, respectively.
source: The best agreement with the experimental data was achieved when ATP (ADP) binding constants were 800 nM (7 μM) and 1 nM (1.5 μM) for the domain-undocked and –docked states, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on fitting thermodynamic model to experimental data.

claim: The ADP-bound and ATP-bound domain-docked conformations are structurally almost identical but thermodynamically different.
source: Intriguingly, while the ADP-bound and ATP-bound domain-docked conformations are structurally almost identical, these two domain-docked conformations are thermodynamically different.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR data showing similar structures but different thermodynamic properties.

claim: Domain docking dramatically favors only ATP binding, while ADP affinity is significantly less affected.
source: First, domain docking dramatically favors only ATP binding, while ADP affinity is significantly less affected (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is based on thermodynamic analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Only ATP but not ADP binding to the AMPylated V461F variant is entropically driven.
source: Moreover, only ATP but not ADP binding to the AMPylated V461F variant is entropically driven (Figure 5—source data 2), suggesting that domain docking is not responsible for the favorable entropic contribution to the free energy of ATP binding.
evidence: This is based on ITC data shown in Figure 5—source data 2.

claim: Domain docking is not responsible for the favorable entropic contribution to the free energy of ATP binding.
source: Moreover, only ATP but not ADP binding to the AMPylated V461F variant is entropically driven (Figure 5—source data 2), suggesting that domain docking is not responsible for the favorable entropic contribution to the free energy of ATP binding.
evidence: This is inferred from thermodynamic data.

claim: The difference in BiP and DnaK thermodynamics of ATP binding is implied by differences in communication between the NBD subdomains.
source: We speculate that this difference in BiP and DnaK thermodynamics of ATP binding is implied by differences in communication between the NBD subdomains.
evidence: This is a speculation based on comparison of thermodynamic data and known structural differences.

claim: The number of structural elements connecting the NBD subdomains varies between different Hsp70s and controls the Hsp70 rate of nucleotide release.
source: It has been shown previously that the number of structural elements (i.e., salt bridges and a hydrophobic patch) connecting the NBD subdomains, varies between different Hsp70s and control the Hsp70 rate of nucleotide release (and their chaperone activity) (Brehmer et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In DnaK, very strong communication between NBD subdomains 'locks' the NBD in one ATP-bound conformation and restricts its conformational flexibility.
source: In DnaK, very strong communication between NBD subdomains apparently 'lock' the NBD in one ATP-bound conformation and thus, restrict its conformational flexibility.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of BiP and DnaK thermodynamic properties.

claim: Weaker communication between the BiP NBD subdomains results in the roughness of the NBD conformational landscape and enhanced NBD conformational flexibility in the presence of ATP.
source: In turn, weaker communication between the BiP NBD subdomains results in the roughness of the NBD conformational landscape and enhanced NBD conformational flexibility in the presence of ATP.
evidence: This is inferred from thermodynamic data showing entropic contribution to ATP binding.

claim: In solution, each Hsp70 chaperone has a complex conformational landscape and co-exists as a heterogeneous ensemble of several conformations.
source: Whilst recent crystallographic descriptions of the ATP-bound states gave an impression that different Hsp70s adopt the same domain-docked and domain-undocked states, growing experimental evidence suggests that in solution each chaperone has a complex conformational landscape and co-exists as a heterogeneous ensemble of several conformations (Zhuravleva et al., 2012; Lai et al., 2017; Marcinowski et al., 2011a; Mapa et al., 2010; Sikor et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and the current study's findings.

claim: The DnaK cycle comprises three functionally and structurally distinct conformations: linker-unbound domain-undocked (U), domain-docked (D), and linker-bound domain-undocked (I).
source: As discussed above, the DnaK cycle comprises three functionally and structurally distinct conformations: (Zhuravleva et al., 2012; Lai et al., 2017) In the ADP-bound state, the chaperone adopts the linker-unbound, domain-undocked conformation (U); ADP-to-ATP exchange results in domain docking and predominant occupancy of the domain-docked conformation (D); and substrate-binding to the ATP-bound state results in domain undocking with population of an ensemble of the ADP-like (but ATP-bound) linker-unbound, domain-undocked conformation (U) and an allosterically active, intermediate linker-bound domain-undocked conformation (I) that has been shown to be essential for efficient substrate binding and release as well as ATPase hydrolysis (Figure 6, left).
evidence: This is a summary of previous work on DnaK supported by citations.

claim: ATP-bound BiP co-exists in solution as an ensemble of two functional states: the domain-docked conformation (D) and an ADP-like (but ATP-bound) domain-undocked conformation (U), interconverting on the relatively slow (hundred millisecond–sub-second) time-scale.
source: However, in contrast to DnaK, ATP-bound BiP co-exists in solution as an ensemble of two functional states: the domain-docked conformation (D) and an ADP-like (but ATP-bound) domain-undocked conformation (U), interconverting on the relatively slow (hundred millisecond–sub-second) time-scale.
evidence: This is based on NMR data showing two sets of peaks and slow exchange.

claim: Substrate binding to ATP-bound BiP stabilizes the linker-unbound, domain-undocked conformation (U), while a small fraction of the domain-docked conformation (D) also co-exists in solution.
source: Substrate binding stabilizes the linker-unbound, domain-undocked conformation (U), while a small fraction of the domain-docked conformation (D) also co-exists in solution.
evidence: This is based on NMR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Interactions between the interdomain linker and NBD are only observed for the isolated NBD or for the domain-docked FL BiP.
source: Interestingly, interactions between the interdomain linker and NBD are only observed for the isolated NBD or for the domain-docked FL BiP, suggesting that the linker-bound conformation (I) is only transiently populated upon domain undocking.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR data comparing different constructs.

claim: The linker-bound conformation (I) is only transiently populated upon domain undocking in BiP.
source: Interestingly, interactions between the interdomain linker and NBD are only observed for the isolated NBD or for the domain-docked FL BiP, suggesting that the linker-bound conformation (I) is only transiently populated upon domain undocking.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR data.

claim: For BiP, the linker-bound conformation is transiently populated even in the absence of ATP.
source: However, ATP binding is not essential for BiP to adopt the domain-docked conformation. This conformation is significantly populated upon AMPylation or other local perturbations of its βSBD even in the ADP-bound state, indicating that for BiP the linker-bound conformation is transiently populated even in the absence of ATP.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR data showing domain docking in ADP-bound state upon mutations or AMPylation.

claim: AMPylation-induced stabilization of domain docking rationalizes the experimentally observed effects of AMPylation on BiP function.
source: This AMPylation-induced stabilization of the domain docking entirely rationalizes the experimentally observed effects of AMPylation on BiP function (Preissler S., Ron D., et al., personal communication, 2017, a co-submitted manuscript).
evidence: This is supported by reference to a co-submitted manuscript.

claim: AMPylation promotes fast substrate release and prevents stimulation of ATP-hydrolysis by J-domain containing co-chaperones.
source: As expected from AMPylation-induced stabilization of the docked state, which is inefficient for ATP hydrolysis and substrate binding, AMPylation promotes fast substrate release and prevents stimulation of ATP-hydrolysis by J-domain containing co-chaperones that observed experimentally by Ron and colleagues.
evidence: This is inferred from the conformational effects of AMPylation and supported by reference to work by Ron and colleagues.

claim: The allosteric model explains enhanced protection of the interdomain linker from proteolysis and linker-promoted oligomerization observed for AMPylated BiP in the presence of both ADP and ATP.
source: Moreover, our allosteric model also explains enhanced protection of the interdomain linker from proteolysis and linker-promoted oligomerization observed for AMPylated BiP in the presence of both ADP and ATP (Preissler S., Ron D., et al., personal communication, 2017, a co-submitted manuscript).
evidence: This is inferred from the conformational model and supported by reference to work by Ron and colleagues.

claim: Local perturbations in the BiP SBD fine-tune the pre-existing conformation ensemble populated upon binding to certain ligands.
source: Our results demonstrate that local perturbations in the BiP SBD fine-tune the pre-existing conformation ensemble populated upon binding to the certain ligands
evidence: This is based on NMR data showing that mutations shift the equilibrium between pre-existing conformations.

claim: An evident correlation exists between the free energy of nucleotide binding and domain docking.
source: An evident correlation between the free energy of nucleotide binding and domain docking (Figure 5B) validates that populations of the domain-docked and -undocked conformations observed in NMR spectra indeed quantitatively represent thermodynamically relevant conformational distributions in the BiP functional ensemble.
evidence: This is based on thermodynamic analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Local perturbations in the BiP SBD may overpower conformational effects of nucleotide binding without decoupling of inter-domain and intra-domain allosteric transitions.
source: Intriguingly, local perturbations in the BiP SBD may also overpower conformational effects of nucleotide binding without decoupling of inter-domain and intra-domain allosteric transitions.
evidence: This is based on NMR data showing domain docking in ADP-bound state for certain mutants.

claim: Local SBD perturbations in BiP preserve the inter-domain allostery and may complement each other.
source: Astonishingly, local SBD perturbations in the BiP SBD preserve the inter-domain allostery in BiP and may also complement each other (Figure 6).
evidence: This is based on NMR data showing additive effects of mutations and AMPylation.

claim: The tunable properties of the BiP conformational landscape provide new opportunities to develop BiP-specific allosteric drugs.
source: While mounting evidence suggests that BiP activity is linked to neurodegenerative diseases, diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, cancer progression and anticancer drug resistance, (Schönthal, 2013; Dudek et al., 2009) these tunable properties of the BiP conformational landscape are particularly interesting because they potentially provide new opportunities to develop BiP-specific allosteric drugs (Nussinov and Tsai, 2013) to enable precise modulations of BiP activity.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential applications based on the findings, supported by citations.

claim: Different members of the Hsp70 family fine-tune their function evolutionally and post-translationally through adjustments of their conformational landscape rather than by altering chaperone structure.
source: Our findings also suggest that different members of the Hsp70 family apparently fine-tune their function evolutionally and post-translationally through adjustments of their conformational landscape rather than by altering chaperone structure.
evidence: This is a general conclusion inferred from the findings about BiP conformational regulation.

claim: The findings present experimental evidence that highlights the role of conformational dynamics in allosteric regulation of complex multidomain systems such as molecular chaperones.
source: More broadly, our findings present experimental evidence that highlights the role of conformational dynamics in allosteric regulation (Wrabl et al., 2011; Guo and Zhou, 2016) of complex multidomain systems such as molecular chaperones.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the broader implications of the work, supported by citations.
